kpg-extinction.summary: An asteroid impact at Chicxulub ended the non-avian dinosaurs and about three quarters of all species, opening the way for mammals.
kpg-extinction.significance: One bad afternoon reset the terms of life on land. Mammals had already existed for 160 million years as small nocturnal animals; the impact is what let them become anything else.

primates.summary: Small tree-dwellers with grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and unusually large brains for their size, radiating in the space left by the dinosaurs.
primates.note: The bracket is the radiation that followed the K-Pg extinction, ending with the first unambiguous true primates in the early Eocene. Primates did not stop in the Eocene; the entry is their arrival, as "First mammals" is the arrival of mammals.

himalayan-orogeny.summary: The Indian plate, having drifted north from Gondwana, collided with Eurasia and drove up the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau. The range is still rising by roughly 5 mm a year.
himalayan-orogeny.significance: Still happening. The collision that raised these mountains also drives the monsoon that waters the subcontinent, which means it underwrites nearly every Indian entry that follows.
himalayan-orogeny.note: Estimates for the onset of continental collision range from about 59 Ma to 50 Ma depending on whether initial contact or full suturing is dated.

sources.title: USGS — The Himalayas: Two continents collide

grasslands-spread.summary: A cooling, drying world replaced forest with open grassland across Africa — the habitat change that put our ancestors on the ground and eventually on two feet.

apes-emerge.summary: The hominoids appear — larger-bodied, tailless, with shoulders built for hanging rather than running along branches.
apes-emerge.note: Molecular and fossil estimates for the catarrhine split range from about 30 to 25 million years ago, with the lineages clearly distinct by roughly 20 Ma. Wikidata gives 20.4 Ma, at the young end.

human-chimp-split.summary: The last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees lived in Africa. Everything human happened in the time since.
human-chimp-split.note: Molecular clocks give a range of roughly 6 to 13 million years depending on assumed mutation rates; the fossil record is sparse.

sahelanthropus.summary: One of the oldest candidates for a hominin, found in Chad, with a skull base hinting at upright posture.
sahelanthropus.note: Whether it walked upright, and whether it sits on our side of the split at all, is still argued from a single distorted skull.

ardipithecus.summary: Walked upright on the ground while keeping a grasping big toe for the trees, showing that bipedalism came before the savannah.

australopithecus.summary: Fully bipedal with an ape-sized brain, known from the skeleton called Lucy and from footprints at Laetoli preserved in volcanic ash. Upright walking came first; the big brain came much later.
australopithecus.significance: Lucy settles an old argument. Walking upright came first and the large brain came two million years later, so bipedalism cannot have been a consequence of intelligence.

laetoli-footprints.summary: Seventy metres of hominin trackway preserved in volcanic ash in northern Tanzania, made by at least three individuals walking upright with a modern heel-strike gait — direct behavioural evidence of bipedalism more than a million years before the first stone tools.
laetoli-footprints.significance: Bones tell you what an animal could do. These tell you what three of them did, one morning, in the rain — which is a different kind of evidence and a much rarer one.
laetoli-footprints.note: Found in 1976 and excavated by Mary Leakey's team over the following two years. The trackmakers are usually taken to be Australopithecus afarensis on grounds of date and place rather than direct association — no bones were in the ash with them.

stone-tools.summary: Deliberately struck sharp flakes, the beginning of a technological record that runs unbroken to the present.
stone-tools.note: The Lomekwi tools at 3.3 Ma predate our genus and are disputed; the Oldowan industry from 2.6 Ma is not.

lucy.summary: An adult female Australopithecus afarensis, about 1.1 metres tall, whose pelvis and knee show she walked upright on a body that still had a brain of roughly 400cc — the most complete early hominin known when she was found, and still the one everybody can name.
lucy.significance: She settled the order of events. Before Lucy the assumption was that the big brain came first and walking upright followed; a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton that walked upright with a brain the size of a chimpanzee's reversed it, and every account since has had to start from that.
lucy.note: Not a missing link, and not a chain. Australopithecus afarensis may be ancestral to our genus or may be a close cousin of whatever was - the fossils do not settle it - and several other hominin species were alive at the same time. She is about forty per cent of one skeleton, found on 24 November 1974 at Hadar in the Afar of Ethiopia by Donald Johanson and Tom Gray, and named after the Beatles song playing in camp that night. Ethiopians call her Dinkinesh: you are marvellous.

sources.title: Institute of Human Origins — Lucy's Story

taung-child.summary: The fossilised skull and brain endocast of a three-year-old, quarried at Taung in South Africa in 1924, whose forward-set foramen magnum showed it had walked upright — the first australopithecine found, and the first evidence that human origins were African.
taung-child.significance: The right answer, published in 1925, and disbelieved for twenty years because a forged skull in England had already convinced Europe that the brain came first and that humans began somewhere other than Africa.
taung-child.note: Raymond Dart described it in Nature in February 1925 as Australopithecus africanus and was dismissed by most of the British establishment. Piltdown Man — a human skull with an orangutan jaw, planted in Sussex — was not exposed as a fake until 1953, by which time other African australopithecines had made Dart's case for him. The specimen's own age is argued, with estimates from about 3 to 2.6 million years.

paranthropus.summary: Robust australopithecines with molars four times the area of ours, jaw muscles anchored to a crest along the skull, and a diet of hard, low quality plant food — living alongside early Homo in eastern and southern Africa for over a million years before vanishing.
paranthropus.significance: A hominin lineage that lasted a million and a half years, chewed its way through the same landscapes as our ancestors, and left no descendants at all. The family tree is a bush, and most of its branches end.
paranthropus.note: Whether the robust australopithecines form one genus or are several separate lineages that converged on the same heavy-chewing anatomy is still argued. Their disappearance has no agreed explanation; competition with early Homo and climate-driven changes in their food plants are both proposed and neither is settled.
